proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(x\in\mathcal X\).  First let \(a\ne a_0\).  For an anchor \(c\in T_{xa}(S)\), put
\[
p_c(t)=y_{cx}-\Gamma(m_c-t)_+,
\qquad q_c(t)=y_{cx}+\Gamma(t-m_c)_+.
\]
The maps \(t\mapsto-(m_c-t)_+\) and \(t\mapsto(t-m_c)_+\) are nondecreasing and one-Lipschitz.  Hence \(p_c\) and \(q_c\) are nondecreasing and \(\Gamma\)-Lipschitz.  A finite maximum or minimum preserves these two properties: if all \(f_j\) have the properties, then for \(s\le t\),
\[
\max_j f_j(s)\leq\max_j f_j(t),
\qquad
\left|\max_j f_j(t)-\max_j f_j(s)\right|
\leq\max_j|f_j(t)-f_j(s)|\leq\Gamma|t-s|,
\]
and the same inequalities follow for a minimum by applying the maximum statement to \(-f_j\).  Constants zero and one have Lipschitz constant zero, so the definitions in \(\mathrm{def{:}envelopes}\) show that both envelopes are nondecreasing and \(\Gamma\)-Lipschitz.

Compatibility means that there is a response schedule \(\widetilde\mu\in\mathcal M_N\) satisfying \(y_{cx}=\widetilde\mu_{xa}(m_c)\) at every matching anchor.  If \(m_c\geq t\), Lipschitz continuity gives
\[
y_{cx}-\Gamma(m_c-t)\leq\widetilde\mu_{xa}(t)\leq y_{cx},
\]
whereas if \(m_c\leq t\), monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity give
\[
y_{cx}\leq\widetilde\mu_{xa}(t)
\leq y_{cx}+\Gamma(t-m_c).
\]
Thus every term in the lower maximum is at most \(\widetilde\mu_{xa}(t)\), and every term in the upper minimum is at least \(\widetilde\mu_{xa}(t)\).  Since \(0\leq\widetilde\mu_{xa}(t)\leq1\),
\[
0\leq\ell_{xa}(t;y)\leq\widetilde\mu_{xa}(t)
\leq u_{xa}(t;y)\leq1.
\]
At an anchor \(d\in T_{xa}(S)\), the \(d\)-term gives \(\ell_{xa}(m_d;y)\geq y_{dx}\) and \(u_{xa}(m_d;y)\leq y_{dx}\); the preceding sandwich gives the reverse inequalities, so both envelopes equal \(y_{dx}\).

For \(a=a_0\), \(\mathrm{ass{:}neutral\text{-}invariance}\) implies that all matching anchor values are the same.  With the prescribed replacement \(\Gamma=0\), the two envelopes equal this common constant when an anchor exists, and equal the constants zero and one when none exists.  They are therefore bounded, constant, agree with every neutral anchor, and satisfy the claimed order.  This proves every assertion.

Let \(Y\in\mathcal M_N\) be compatible with \(y\), and write \(\mu\) for its finite-population conditional mean surface.  The anchor inequalities proved in \(\mathrm{lem{:}envelope\text{-}feasibility}\) apply componentwise and give, for every \(\pi\in\mathcal F\),
\[
L_S(\pi;y)
=\sum_xq_x\ell_{x,\pi(x)}(m_\pi;y)
\leq\sum_xq_x\mu_{x,\pi(x)}(m_\pi)
=V_\mu(\pi)
\leq\sum_xq_xu_{x,\pi(x)}(m_\pi;y)
=U_S(\pi;y),
\]
where positivity of the finite-population weights \(q_x=N_x/N\) preserves the inequalities.

Define two complete response surfaces, simultaneously for every cell and action, by
\[
\mu^-_{xa}(t)=\ell_{xa}(t;y),
\qquad
\mu^+_{xa}(t)=u_{xa}(t;y).
\]
The envelope-feasibility lemma says that these surfaces take values in \([0,1]\), are nondecreasing and \(\Gamma\)-Lipschitz for nonneutral actions, are constant for the neutral action, and reproduce every selected mean.  For every unit \(i\) in cell \(x_i=x\), set
\[
Y_i^-(a,t)=\mu^-_{xa}(t),
\qquad Y_i^+(a,t)=\mu^+_{xa}(t).
\]
Because \(N_x>0\), averaging either fixed array over the units in cell \(x\) returns the displayed surface.  Thus both arrays belong to \(\mathcal M_N\), and they induce the same table \(y\).  By the definition of policy value,
\[
V_{\mu^-}(\pi)=L_S(\pi;y),
\qquad
V_{\mu^+}(\pi)=U_S(\pi;y)
\quad\text{for every }\pi\in\mathcal F.
\]
These are the two common endpoint schedules.

It remains to show that there are no gaps inside a scalar identified set.  The response class and the anchor equalities are convex.  Hence for \(\lambda\in[0,1]\),
\[
\mu^\lambda=(1-\lambda)\mu^-+\lambda\mu^+
\]
is compatible and belongs to \(\mathcal M_N\), and linearity of the finite-population value gives
\[
V_{\mu^\lambda}(\pi)
=(1-\lambda)L_S(\pi;y)+\lambda U_S(\pi;y).
\]
As \(\lambda\) ranges over \([0,1]\), this fills the entire closed interval.  Together with the first sandwich, the identified set is exactly the asserted interval.

Fix \(S\in\mathcal P_k\), a compatible table \(y\), a future policy \(\pi\), and a cell \(x\).  Write \(a=\pi(x)\) and \(t=m_\pi\).  If there is no matching-action anchor, boundedness gives
\[
u_{xa}(t;y)-\ell_{xa}(t;y)\leq1=r_{\pi x}(S).
\]
If \(a=a_0\) and a matching anchor exists, neutral invariance makes the gap zero, again equal to \(r_{\pi x}(S)\).  Otherwise, for any matching nonneutral anchor \(c\), if \(m_c\leq t\), the envelope definitions imply
\[
\ell_{xa}(t;y)\geq y_{cx},
\qquad
u_{xa}(t;y)\leq y_{cx}+\Gamma(t-m_c),
\]
and if \(m_c\geq t\), they imply
\[
\ell_{xa}(t;y)\geq y_{cx}-\Gamma(m_c-t),
\qquad
u_{xa}(t;y)\leq y_{cx}.
\]
After also using the unit bound, both cases yield
\[
u_{xa}(t;y)-\ell_{xa}(t;y)
\leq\min\{1,\Gamma|t-m_c|\}.
\]
Taking the minimum over matching anchors gives the corresponding \(r_{\pi x}(S)\).  Summing with \(q_x>0\) and maximizing over the finite set \(\mathcal F\) proves
\[
\sup_{Y\in\mathcal M_N}\max_{\pi\in\mathcal F}
\{U_S(\pi;y(Y))-L_S(\pi;y(Y))\}
\leq\max_{\pi\in\mathcal F}R_\pi(S).
\]

For the reverse inequality, choose \(\pi^\star\) attaining the finite maximum on the right.  For each \(x\), put \(a=\pi^\star(x)\), \(t=m_{\pi^\star}\), and \(w=r_{\pi^\star x}(S)\).  If \(a\ne a_0\), there are three cases.  With no matching anchor, take \(g_x^-=0\) and \(g_x^+=1\).  With a matching anchor and \(w=0\), take both functions to be zero.  With \(w>0\), necessarily \(\Gamma>0\), and define
\[
g_x^-(s)=\min\{w,\max\{0,\Gamma(s-t)\}\},
\qquad
g_x^+(s)=\min\{w,\max\{0,\Gamma(s-t)+w\}\}.
\]
Clipping is nondecreasing and one-Lipschitz, so these functions are bounded, nondecreasing, and \(\Gamma\)-Lipschitz.  Every matching selected score \(m_c\) satisfies \(\Gamma|m_c-t|\geq w\).  If \(m_c<t\), both displayed functions are zero there; if \(m_c>t\), both are \(w\) there.  The equality case \(m_c=t\) would force \(w=0\), already handled.  Thus the functions agree at all matching anchors, while
\[
g_x^-(t)=0,
\qquad g_x^+(t)=w.
\]
If \(a=a_0\), take identical zero constants when a matching anchor exists, and take the two constants zero and one otherwise.  These choices likewise agree at every selected neutral anchor and differ at the target by \(w\).

For each cell, use \(g_x^-\) and \(g_x^+\) for the target action \(a\), and use the same zero function in the two schedules for every other action.  Set every individual potential outcome in a cell equal to its corresponding cell surface.  This constructs two fixed arrays \(Y^-\) and \(Y^+\) in \(\mathcal M_N\).  At every selected arm-cell pair the arrays agree: for the target action this is the anchor equality just proved, and for another action both values are zero.  Let \(y^\star\) be their common selected table.  Their causal values at \(\pi^\star\) satisfy
\[
V_{\mu^+}(\pi^\star)-V_{\mu^-}(\pi^\star)
=\sum_xq_xw
=R_{\pi^\star}(S).
\]
By \(\mathrm{thm{:}sharp\text{-}common\text{-}endpoints}\), both values lie in the same sharp interval generated by \(y^\star\), so its width is at least this difference.  The established upper bound forces equality.  Therefore the supremum is attained by these two observationally indistinguishable fixed arrays and
\[
\overline W(S)=\max_{\pi\in\mathcal F}R_\pi(S)
=\max_{\pi\in\mathcal F}\sum_xq_x
\min\bigl(\{1\}\cup\{d_{\pi xc}:c\in S\}\bigr).
\]
All costs and weights are rational, and the maximum and minimum range over finite sets.  Since \(\mathcal P_k\) is finite and contains the empty panel, its minimum is rational and attained.  This proves the final assertion about \(D^\star\).

Fix an integral selection vector \(z\) and let \(S_z=\{c:z_c=1\}\).  The budget constraint gives \(S_z\in\mathcal P_k\).  For each pair \((\pi,x)\), the constraints \(b_{\pi xc}\leq z_c\), nonnegativity, and normalization imply that \((b_{\pi xc})\) is a convex combination supported on \(S_z\cup\{\varnothing\}\).  Consequently
\[
\sum_{c\in\mathcal C\cup\{\varnothing\}}d_{\pi xc}b_{\pi xc}
\geq \min\bigl(\{1\}\cup\{d_{\pi xc}:c\in S_z\}\bigr)
=r_{\pi x}(S_z).
\]
The scenario constraint therefore forces \(v\geq R_\pi(S_z)\) for every \(\pi\), and hence
\[
v\geq\max_{\pi\in\mathcal F}R_\pi(S_z).
\]
Conversely, for each \((\pi,x)\), choose one cheapest element of \(S_z\cup\{\varnothing\}\), put its \(b\)-coordinate equal to one, and put all other coordinates equal to zero.  This is feasible and turns the last display into equality for every cell.  The smallest feasible \(v\) is therefore \(\max_\pi R_\pi(S_z)\).  Minimizing over all integral \(z\) and invoking \(\mathrm{thm{:}width\text{-}identity}\) gives
\[
\operatorname{val}(\mathsf P_{\mathrm{MILP}})
=\min_{S\in\mathcal P_k}\max_\pi R_\pi(S)
=\min_{S\in\mathcal P_k}\overline W(S)
=D^\star.
\]
No integrality of \(b\) is needed because an extreme cheapest-coordinate assignment already attains the conditional minimum.

The width identity first gives the monotonicity used by the checker.  If \(S\subseteq S'\), then each minimum is taken over a larger set for \(S'\), so
\[
r_{\pi x}(S')\leq r_{\pi x}(S),
\qquad R_\pi(S')\leq R_\pi(S),
\qquad \overline W(S')\leq\overline W(S).
\]

Suppose the checker accepts.  Its direct tests give \(S^\star\in\mathcal P_k\) and the exact rational equality \(\overline W(S^\star)=v^\star\).  At a node \((I,E,O)\), its two verified children partition the descendants \(S\) satisfying \(I\subseteq S\subseteq I\cup E\) according as the branched candidate belongs to \(S\).  Induction from the root therefore shows that every subset of \(\mathcal C\), and hence every feasible panel, reaches a leaf.  A leaf with \(|I|>k\) has no feasible descendant because every descendant contains \(I\).  At any other accepted leaf, the checker has recomputed
\[
\overline W(I\cup E)\geq v^\star.
\]
Every descendant \(S\) obeys \(S\subseteq I\cup E\), so the monotonicity just proved gives
\[
\overline W(S)\geq\overline W(I\cup E)\geq v^\star.
\]
Thus all feasible panels have loss at least \(v^\star\), while the checked incumbent has loss exactly \(v^\star\).  It follows from the definition of \(D^\star\) that
\[
D^\star=v^\star=\overline W(S^\star).
\]
This conclusion is derived from the accepted local checks; it is not a field asserted inside the certificate.

Conversely, on a rational instance enumerate the finite family \(\mathcal P_k\), recompute every width by the rational formula in the width identity, choose a minimizing panel \(S^\star\), and set \(v^\star=\overline W(S^\star)\).  Starting from the required root, repeatedly branch on any fixed-order element of \(E\).  Close a path immediately if \(|I|>k\); otherwise continue until \(E=\varnothing\).  At such a terminal node, \(I\) is feasible and optimality of the enumerated incumbent gives
\[
\overline W(I\cup E)=\overline W(I)\geq v^\star,
\]
which is precisely the optimistic-bound leaf rule.  The depth is at most \(|\mathcal C|\), so this construction terminates in a finite tree.  Every arithmetic operation is a minimum, maximum, sum, or comparison of input rationals.  Hence the exact checker accepts this certificate, proving completeness, although the exhaustive tree may have exponential size.

Let the metric space be the disjoint union of all clients and eligible facilities.  Set the distance from a point to itself to zero, make the displayed cross-distance symmetric, and set the distance between distinct points of the same type to two.  Because \(0\leq d_{\pi xc}\leq1\), every distance between distinct points lies in \([1,2]\).  Positivity, symmetry, and separation are immediate.  For three distinct points \(p,q,r\),
\[
\delta(p,q)\leq2\leq\delta(p,r)+\delta(r,q),
\]
and triangles with a repeated point are tautological.  Thus \(\delta\) is a metric.

For nonempty \(S\), all selected costs are at most one, so the dummy in the definition of \(r\) does not change their minimum.  The scenario-\(\pi\) nearest-facility cost is therefore
\[
\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}q_x\min_{c\in S}\delta(j_{\pi x},f_c)
=\sum_xq_x\left(1+\min_{c\in S}d_{\pi xc}\right)
=\sum_xq_x+R_\pi(S)
=1+R_\pi(S).
\]
Here \(\sum_xq_x=N^{-1}\sum_xN_x=1\), since the cells partition the \(N\) units.  The representation retains only candidate facilities, uses rational client weights, and represents the at-most budget and empty-panel fallback by conventions outside the literal unweighted exactly-\(k\) formulation.  Hence the asserted exact lift and its stated boundary from the comparator follow.

Take an instance of maximum \(k\)-coverage with a nonempty universe \(\mathcal X\) of size \(M\) and a family of distinct subsets \((B_c)_{c\in\mathcal C}\); duplicate subsets, if any, can first be deleted without changing the optimum.  Set \(q_x=1/M\), \(\mathcal A=\{0,1\}\), \(a_0=0\), and \(\Gamma=0\).  Use one future policy \(\pi\) with \(\pi(x)=1\) for every \(x\), and define each candidate by
\[
c(x)=\begin{cases}1,&x\in B_c,\\0,&x\notin B_c.\end{cases}
\]
All scores may be set to zero.  This construction has size polynomial in the incidence description of the coverage instance.  By \(\mathrm{def{:}score\text{-}cost}\),
\[
d_{\pi xc}=\begin{cases}0,&x\in B_c,\\1,&x\notin B_c.\end{cases}
\]
The width identity then gives, for every panel \(S\),
\[
\overline W(S)
=\frac1M\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}
\mathbf1\{x\notin\bigcup_{c\in S}B_c\}
=1-\frac1M\left|\bigcup_{c\in S}B_c\right|.
\]
Thus a selection covers at least \(B\) universe elements if and only if its width is at most \(1-B/M\).  The cited NP-hardness of maximum \(k\)-coverage therefore transfers through this polynomial reduction to exact computation of \(D^\star\), under all the restrictions stated in the proposition.

For \(S=\varnothing\), every anchor set is empty.  The envelope definitions, including the neutral-action convention, reduce to
\[
\ell_{xa}(t;\varnothing)=0,
\qquad u_{xa}(t;\varnothing)=1
\quad\text{for every }x,a,t.
\]
Since the cells partition \(\mathcal I\),
\[
\sum_xq_x=\frac1N\sum_xN_x=1.
\]
Consequently \(L_\varnothing(\pi;\varnothing)=0\), \(U_\varnothing(\pi;\varnothing)=1\), and the sharp-common-endpoints theorem gives the exact identified interval \([0,1]\).  Equivalently, the width identity has \(r_{\pi x}(\varnothing)=1\) in every cell and therefore yields \(\overline W(\varnothing)=1\).  No positive allocation exists for an empty arm set, so this calculation uses only fixed potential outcomes and contains no assignment distribution.

Fix \(c\in S\) and \(x\in\mathcal X\), and define the fixed numbers
\[
w_i=\mathbf1\{x_i=x\}Y_i(c(x_i),m_c)\in[0,1].
\]
Their finite-population mean is
\[
\frac1N\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}w_i
=\frac{N_x}{N}\frac1{N_x}\sum_{i:x_i=x}Y_i(c(x),m_c)
=q_xy_{cx}.
\]
Under complete randomization, the marginal set \(A_c=\{i:Z_i=c\}\) is a uniformly chosen \(n_c\)-subset of \(\mathcal I\).  Moreover, on \(A_c\), consistency in the definition of \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\) gives \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=Y_i(c(x_i),m_c)\).  Hence
\[
\widehat y_{cx}^{\mathrm{HT}}
=\frac1{q_x}\frac1{n_c}\sum_{i\in A_c}w_i.
\]
Apply \(\mathrm{lem{:}hoeffding\text{-}sampling\text{-}without\text{-}replacement}\) with
\[
t_{cx}=\sqrt{\frac{\log(2J/\alpha)}{2n_c}},
\qquad J=|S||\mathcal X|>0.
\]
Because \(q_x>0\), division is valid, and it gives
\[
\Pr_Z\!\left(
\left|\widehat y_{cx}^{\mathrm{HT}}-y_{cx}\right|>
q_x^{-1}t_{cx}
\right)
\leq2e^{-2n_ct_{cx}^2}=\frac{\alpha}{J}.
\]
A union bound over the exactly \(J\) arm-cell pairs yields an event \(\mathcal E\) with \(\Pr_Z(\mathcal E)\geq1-\alpha\) on which every un-clipped interval \([\widehat y_{cx}^{\mathrm{HT}}-\varepsilon_{cx},\widehat y_{cx}^{\mathrm{HT}}+\varepsilon_{cx}]\) contains \(y_{cx}\).  Since \(0\leq y_{cx}\leq1\), clipping its lower endpoint upward to at least zero and its upper endpoint downward to at most one preserves containment.  Thus on \(\mathcal E\),
\[
l_{cx}\leq y_{cx}\leq h_{cx}
\quad\text{simultaneously for all }(c,x).
\]

Each expression \(\ell_{xa}(t;\cdot)\) is a maximum of coordinatewise nondecreasing affine functions of the relevant anchors, and each \(u_{xa}(t;\cdot)\) is a minimum of such functions.  Both are therefore coordinatewise nondecreasing, including under the neutral convention.  Positive weighted summation gives on \(\mathcal E\)
\[
L_S(\pi;l)\leq L_S(\pi;y),
\qquad U_S(\pi;y)\leq U_S(\pi;h)
\quad\text{for every }\pi\in\mathcal F.
\]
The sharp-common-endpoints theorem supplies \(L_S(\pi;y)\leq U_S(\pi;y)\), so
\[
[L_S(\pi;y),U_S(\pi;y)]
\subseteq[L_S(\pi;l),U_S(\pi;h)]
=\mathcal O_S(\pi)
\]
simultaneously over the whole future library.  The sole probability event was indexed by the \(J\) primitive arm-cell means, so there is no further factor involving \(|\mathcal F|\).  The bound used only fixed \([0,1]\)-valued arrays and the assignment law, and is consequently uniform over \(\mathcal M_N\).  Its construction requires \(S\ne\varnothing\), as stated.

When \(\Gamma=0\), the three cases in \(\mathrm{def{:}score\text{-}cost}\) give
\[
d_{\pi xc}=\begin{cases}
0,&c(x)=\pi(x),\\
1,&c(x)\ne\pi(x).
\end{cases}
\]
Indeed, a matching neutral action is assigned zero explicitly, and a matching nonneutral action has \(\min\{1,0\}=0\).  Therefore
\[
r_{\pi x}(S)
=\mathbf1\{c(x)\ne\pi(x)\text{ for every }c\in S\}.
\]
Substitution in the width identity proves
\[
\overline W(S)=\max_{\pi\in\mathcal F}\sum_xq_x
\mathbf1\{c(x)\ne\pi(x)\text{ for every }c\in S\}.
\]
If every pair \((\pi,x)\) has a matching selected candidate, every indicator is zero and hence the width is zero.

All quantities can be audited from the cost vectors.  In candidate order \((c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4,c_5)\), the three cell costs are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
&c_1&c_2&c_3&c_4&c_5\\ \hline
\pi_1&(0,0,1)&(1,0,0)&(1/4,1,1)&(1,1,1/4)&(1,1/4,1)\\
\pi_2&(1/4,1,1)&(1,1,1/4)&(0,0,1)&(1,0,0)&(1,1,1)
\end{array}
\]
by direct substitution into \(d_{\pi xc}\).  Taking coordinatewise minima over each panel and dotting with \((1/6,1/3,1/2)\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\,,\,}c|c}
S&R_{\pi_1}(S)&R_{\pi_2}(S)&\overline W(S)\\ \hline
\varnothing&1&1&1\\
\{c_1\}&1/2&7/8&7/8\\
\{c_2\}&1/6&5/8&5/8\\
\{c_3\}&7/8&1/2&7/8\\
\{c_4\}&5/8&1/6&5/8\\
\{c_5\}&3/4&1&1\\
\{c_1,c_2\}&0&1/2&1/2\\
\{c_1,c_3\}&1/2&1/2&1/2\\
\{c_1,c_4\}&1/8&1/24&1/8\\
\{c_1,c_5\}&1/2&7/8&7/8\\
\{c_2,c_3\}&1/24&1/8&1/8\\
\{c_2,c_4\}&1/6&1/6&1/6\\
\{c_2,c_5\}&1/6&5/8&5/8\\
\{c_3,c_4\}&1/2&0&1/2\\
\{c_3,c_5\}&5/8&1/2&5/8\\
\{c_4,c_5\}&3/8&1/6&3/8
\end{array}
\]
For example, for \(S=\{c_1,c_4\}\), the residual vectors are \((0,0,1/4)\) and \((1/4,0,0)\), giving \(1/8\) and \(1/24\).  The table exhausts all panels of size at most two, so its minimum is \(1/8\), attained exactly by the two stated panels.  The width identity and MILP equivalence then give \(D^\star=\operatorname{val}(\mathsf P_{\mathrm{MILP}})=1/8\).

For the displayed response schedules, every component is bounded, nondecreasing, and one-Lipschitz; the neutral components are constant.  At score \(1/2\), the action-one responses in cells one and two are zero, matching \(c_1\), and at score \(3/4\), the action-one response in cell three is \(1/4\), matching \(c_4\); all selected neutral means are zero.  Thus both schedules lie in \(\mathcal M_N\) and produce the same displayed \(y\).  Direct evaluation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
V_{\mu^-}(\pi_1)&=0,
&V_{\mu^+}(\pi_1)&=(1/2)(1/4)=1/8,\\
V_{\mu^-}(\pi_2)&=(1/2)(1/4)=1/8,
&V_{\mu^+}(\pi_2)&=(1/6)(1/4)+(1/2)(1/4)=1/6.
\end{aligned}
\]
The sharp-common-endpoints theorem identifies these as the simultaneous endpoint intervals claimed.

Finally, the paths \(111\), \(1101\), and \(0111\) have three forced inclusions and are infeasible for \(k=2\).  For the other five leaves, the optimistic panels \(I\cup E\) are respectively
\[
\{c_1,c_2,c_5\},\quad
\{c_1,c_3,c_4,c_5\},\quad
\{c_2,c_3,c_5\},\quad
\{c_2,c_4,c_5\},\quad
\{c_3,c_4,c_5\},
\]
and the same coordinate-minimum calculation gives worst widths
\[
1/2,\qquad1/8,\qquad1/8,\qquad1/6,\qquad1/4.
\]
Every value is at least the recomputed incumbent value \(1/8\).  The least-index binary paths partition all subsets, so every leaf rule, branch relation, root label, and incumbent check in \(\mathsf{Check}\) succeeds.  Hence \(\mathsf{Check}(S^\star,1/8,\mathcal T_{3,5})=\mathrm{true}\).

theorem.statement: There is a deterministic exact-rational realization of \(\mathsf{Handle}\) that, on every rational instance, returns a certificate accepted by the independently specified \(\mathsf{Check}\), and acceptance proves that its incumbent attains \(D^\star\).  The generator and exhaustive enumeration agree exactly on every instance, hence in particular on every three-cell instance with at most five candidates.  Moreover, if \(k\geq1\) and there is a candidate \(c^\dagger\in\mathcal C\) satisfying \(d_{\pi x c^\dagger}\leq d_{\pi xc}\) for every \(\pi\in\mathcal F\), \(x\in\mathcal X\), and \(c\in\mathcal C\), then \(\{c^\dagger\}\) has a one-leaf certificate; its encoded size and its generation and checking time are polynomial in \(|\mathcal C|+|\mathcal F|+|\mathcal X|\).  No polynomial-size guarantee is asserted without such structure.
theorem.proof_tex:
Order the candidates once and for all.  A deterministic generator first computes, in exact rational arithmetic, \(\overline W(S)\) from the width identity for every \(S\in\mathcal P_k\), chooses the lexicographically first minimizer \(S^\star\), and sets \(v^\star=\overline W(S^\star)\).  It then applies the deterministic recursion
\[
G(I,E,O)=
\begin{cases}
\text{a leaf},& |I|>k,\\
\text{a leaf},& \overline W(I\cup E)\geq v^\star,\\
\text{the two recursive children obtained from the least }c\in E,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
The second case must occur when \(E=\varnothing\) and \(|I|\leq k\), because enumeration gives \(\overline W(I)\geq v^\star\).  Thus the recursion terminates after depth at most \(|\mathcal C|\), and every leaf has exactly one of the justifications allowed by \(\mathrm{def{:}certificate\text{-}grammar}\).  The independent checker uses only the original rational instance and the emitted tuple: it recomputes the incumbent width and every leaf bound, verifies the root and each pair of children, and accepts only exact rational equalities and inequalities.  Certificate soundness and completeness therefore imply that acceptance derives \(\overline W(S^\star)=D^\star\).  Because both enumeration and the generator use the same explicitly proved rational functional, their outputs agree exactly for every finite instance, including all instances with three cells and at most five candidates.

For the structural clause, suppose a globally dominating column \(c^\dagger\) exists and \(k\geq1\).  For every \((\pi,x)\),
\[
\min_{c\in\mathcal C}d_{\pi xc}=d_{\pi x c^\dagger}.
\]
Therefore the width identity yields
\[
\overline W(\mathcal C)=\overline W(\{c^\dagger\}).
\]
Since adding candidates cannot increase width, the singleton \(\{c^\dagger\}\) is optimal.  At the root, the exact optimistic-descendant bound is already
\[
\overline W(\varnothing\cup\mathcal C)
=\overline W(\{c^\dagger\})=v^\star,
\]
so the root itself is a valid bound leaf.  Testing dominance takes \(O(|\mathcal C||\mathcal F||\mathcal X|)\) rational comparisons, and computing its width takes \(O(|\mathcal C||\mathcal F||\mathcal X|)\) rational operations; the certificate has one tree node plus the encoded incumbent.  This is polynomial in the stated dimensions.  Identical cost columns are a special case, while the NP-hardness proposition explains why this structural result is not promoted to an unrestricted polynomial-time claim.

Let \(w_1,\ldots,w_N\in[0,1]\) be fixed, and let \(A\) be a uniformly random subset of \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\) of fixed size \(n\geq1\).  Then, for every \(t>0\),
\[
\Pr\!\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_{i\in A}w_i-N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Nw_i\right|\geq t\right)
\leq2\exp(-2nt^2).
\]
